title: Where Are You?
paragraphs:
Where Are You?
The Lesson I Learned From God’s Question to Adam
There are questions that seek information.
Then there are questions that expose the soul.
The first question God asks humanity in Scripture belongs to the second category.
It was not asked because God lacked knowledge.
It was asked because Adam had lost something far greater than his location.
He had lost himself.
And if we're honest, many of us know exactly what that feels like.
Not physically lost.
Spiritually lost.
Emotionally lost.
Lost beneath success.
Lost beneath addiction.
Lost beneath ministry.
Lost beneath achievement.
Lost beneath carefully crafted social media smiles.
Lost beneath the exhausting performance of pretending everything is fine.
The story begins in Genesis 3, immediately after humanity's first rebellion.
Adam and Eve had walked with God in perfect fellowship. There was no shame. No fear. No hiding. No separation.
Then sin entered the garden.
The Hebrew text says they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden.

"וַיִּשְׁמְעוּ אֶת־קוֹל יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים"
(Vayishme'u et-qol Yahweh Elohim)
"Then they heard the voice of the LORD God..." (Genesis 3:8)
For the first time, what once brought comfort now brought terror.
The sound of God's presence had not changed.
They had.
The text says Adam and Eve hid themselves among the trees.
Think about that.
The ones made from dust were attempting to hide from the One who created dust.
The created was hiding from the Creator.
The finite was hiding from the Infinite.
The broken was hiding from the only One who could heal the brokenness.
And then comes one of the most astonishing moments in all Scripture.
Genesis 3:9 says:

"וַיִּקְרָא יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים אֶל־הָאָדָם וַיֹּאמֶר לוֹ אַיֶּכָּה"
(Vayiqra Yahweh Elohim el-ha'adam vayomer lo ayyekkah)
"But the LORD God called to the man and said to him, 'Where are you?'"
The Hebrew word is:

אַיֶּכָּה
(Ayyekkah)
"Where are you?"
This was not a geographical question.
God knew exactly where Adam was standing.
The omniscient Creator had not suddenly lost track of His creation.
This was a relational question.
A spiritual question.
A heart question.
Adam, where are you now?
Where are you compared to where I created you to be?
Where are you compared to the intimacy we once shared?
Where are you compared to the freedom you once knew?
Where are you compared to the innocence you have now traded for shame?
That question echoes through every generation.
It echoes through boardrooms.
Through churches.
Through bedrooms.
Through hospitals.
Through prison cells.
Through funeral homes.
Through addiction recovery meetings.
Through sleepless nights.
Through moments nobody else sees.
Where are you?
Not physically.
Spiritually.
The terrifying reality is that many people spend years answering questions God never asked while avoiding the one He did.
How much money do you make?
How successful are you?
How many followers do you have?
How impressive is your ministry?
How respected is your reputation?
How polished is your image?
God bypasses all of it.
Where are you?
Because before God addresses behavior, He addresses relationship.
Before He addresses consequences, He addresses separation.
Before He addresses the fall, He addresses the distance.
The tragedy of Genesis 3 is not merely that Adam sinned.
It is that Adam hid.
And humanity has been hiding ever since.
Some hide behind religion.
Some hide behind intellect.
Some hide behind accomplishments.
Some hide behind busyness.
Some hide behind trauma.
Some hide behind bitterness.
Some hide behind wounds that were never healed.
Some hide behind a version of themselves they created because they fear who they really are.
Yet the beautiful scandal of the Gospel is this:
God comes looking.
Adam was not searching for God.
God was searching for Adam.
That changes everything.
The Gospel does not begin with humanity climbing toward God.
It begins with God moving toward humanity.
From Genesis to Revelation, this becomes the consistent story of redemption.
The Shepherd pursuing the lost sheep.
The Father running toward the prodigal son.
The Savior entering a fallen world.
The King wearing a crown of thorns.
The innocent dying for the guilty.
The righteous pursuing the unrighteous.
The holy pursuing the unholy.
The Gospel is not the story of seekers finding God.
It is the story of God finding seekers.
The Apostle Paul writes:
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we became worthy.
Not after we fixed our mess.
While we were still sinners.
The footsteps heard in Eden eventually became footsteps walking the roads of Galilee.
The voice calling "Where are you?" eventually became flesh.
The eternal Word entered human history.
The Greek text of John 1:14 says:

"Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο"
(Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto)
"And the Word became flesh."
Jesus Christ is God's ultimate answer to humanity's hiding.
Every page of Scripture moves toward Him.
Every promise points toward Him.
Every sacrifice foreshadows Him.
Every prophecy anticipates Him.
And nowhere is this more visible than at the cross.
At Calvary, Jesus experienced what Adam feared.
Separation.
Abandonment.
Judgment.
The cry from the cross in Aramaic was:

"ܐܠܗܝ ܐܠܗܝ ܠܡܢܐ ܫܒܩܬܢܝ"
(Elohi, Elohi, l'mana shbaqtani)
"My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Mark 15:34)
The One who never sinned entered the consequences of sin.
The One who never hid was abandoned so that those who hide could be restored.
The One who deserved glory accepted shame so that those filled with shame could receive grace.
This is the scandal.
This is why our theme matters.
Adam's story could have ended in judgment alone.
Your story could have ended in judgment alone.
Mine too.
But God writes redemption into ruined chapters.
He specializes in rewriting endings.
The adulterer becomes forgiven.
The addict becomes restored.
The broken become healed.
The prodigal comes home.
The ashamed become accepted.
The guilty become redeemed.
The lost become found.
The cross stands as eternal proof that God is not afraid of your mess.
He already knows where you are.
The question remains:
Do you?
Where are you today?
Not where people think you are.
Not where your profile says you are.
Not where your résumé says you are.
Not where your reputation says you are.
Where are you really?
The invitation of Genesis 3 is not merely self-examination.
It is surrender.
The God who asked Adam "Where are you?" is the same God who extends mercy through Jesus Christ.
The question was never intended to drive Adam away.
It was intended to bring him back.
That same invitation remains open today.
For the believer who feels distant.
For the prodigal who wandered.
For the skeptic who is searching.
For the exhausted soul who has been pretending too long.
For the wounded heart carrying secret burdens.
For the person reading these words and realizing they have spent years hiding among modern trees.
God is still calling.
Where are you?
And even more remarkably:
Will you come out of hiding?
What part of your life has God been calling out of hiding?
Comment, "No more hiding," if you're ready to step into the light of Christ.
Comment, "Pray for me," if you've been carrying burdens in secret.
Comment, "Jesus found me," if you know what it feels like to be pursued by grace.
Your testimony may become someone else's turning point.
Because somewhere between the hiding place and the Father's voice is the moment your life begins again.
